card.hook: Most concert halls try to look like palaces. This one looks like it's about to clock in for a shift, all brick, steel and glass, and that's exactly why it photographs so well.
card.stand_here: Stand in Military Park, on the side facing Park Place, with NJPAC straight across the street. Face the facade and let it fill the middle of your picture.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the facade and the street in one shot. If trees or people are in the way, try 0.5x to fit in more buildings, and use 2x or more (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the brick and glass.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Soft, even daylight gives the brick its best colour. Around dusk, when the building's lights come on, try night mode and hold the phone very still.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little above eye level. Turn so the building sits over your shoulder and tilt the phone until you can see it behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Military Park is a public park, but check its current state before you go. If you'd like to see inside NJPAC, check the official NJPAC site first.
card.challenge: Find a tree branch or trunk at the edge of your screen and use it as a natural frame, with the high-rises standing behind the building.
card.good_to_know: NJPAC opened in October 1997 on the site of the former Military Park Hotel. It's one of the largest performing arts centres in the United States and the home of the New Jersey Symphony Orchestra. Architect Barton Myers chose brick, exposed steel and glass to echo Newark's industrial past.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Military Park, on the side facing Park Place, with NJPAC straight across the street. Face the facade and let it fill the middle of your picture.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific selfie spot or photo-taking position with the New Jersey Performing Arts Center behind the visitor, so I have not listed any spots. Pages I checked: Yelp's NJPAC listing (https://www.yelp.com/biz/new-jersey-performing-arts-center-newark), Visit NJPAC (https://www.njpac.org/visit/), and the Yelp and Travel Lens photo-spot roundups for Newark, which do not include NJPAC as a named spot. The Visit NJPAC page only has a photo caption describing a crowd outside a concert on the plaza, which is not a named selfie spot. The Wikimedia photo of NJPAC has camera coordinates but no named spot. Prudential Center pages (for example the Wikimedia Edison Place photo) describe a different building, so I excluded them. No page gave selfie stick or tripod rules or a safety point for this site. A next step would be a search for NJPAC's own photo guidance or a local blog on Center Street or Military Park views.

card.hook: Here's the twist: the stadium called Newark's is actually in Harrison, and from this park you might not see its roof at all. Think of it as a treasure hunt with a nice river view as the consolation prize.
card.stand_here: Stand in East Newark Riverfront Park, at the corner of Clay St and Passaic Ave, and face south-east. The stadium is a little over two kilometres away in that direction.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the river and sky, then 1x for a balanced shot of the water and skyline. If the curved roof shows up between the buildings, try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick it out. It will be small and distant.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the river along the lower third, and tap the water or the roof so it stays sharp.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon is worth trying for softer light on the water. On match days the area around the stadium gets busy, so check the fixture list before you pick a time.
card.selfie_here: Try the Harrison Riverwalk along the Passaic River, the paved path beside the water, which has views of the Newark skyline. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the river behind you, and check on the spot whether the stadium area makes it into the frame.
card.ask_someone: Over on the Orange Boardwalk paths in Riverfront Park (Ironbound, Newark), stand facing north across the water toward the Harrison bank and ask a passer-by to take your photo there.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is a public riverside space. Check the official site before you go if you want to get into the stadium, especially on match days.
card.challenge: Find the roof's curve between the buildings, then get it on a gridline crossing with a bit of river in front.
card.good_to_know: The stadium opened in 2010 as Red Bull Arena and took the name Sports Illustrated Stadium in December 2024. It's home to the New York Red Bulls and Gotham FC. Its curved fabric roof covers all 25,000 seats, and about 60 feet (18 m) of it lets daylight through.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in East Newark Riverfront Park, at the corner of Clay St and Passaic Ave, and face south-east. The stadium is a little over two kilometres away in that direction.

selfie_spots.detail: on the paved riverside walkway in Harrison, the stretch that runs beside the river and the waterfront
selfie_spots.why: The walkway is described as a scenic path with views of the Newark skyline and the water, so it is a likely place to stand with the river and stadium area behind you, though the pages do not confirm the stadium is in frame.

No page I found names a specific selfie point with the stadium framed behind a visitor, so the selfie spot is inferred from riverside walkway descriptions and should be checked on the ground. The ask-someone spot is only said to be a place where the stadium 'may be seen'; no page confirms the whole stadium is framed from there. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules, or any safety point, for this site.

card.hook: A 22-foot stainless steel hockey player is standing guard in Newark, and he's the best photo prop in town. Put him next to a giant arena that locals call "The Rock" and your photo explains itself.
card.stand_here: Stand in Championship Plaza on Mulberry Street, between Edison Place and Market Street, right beside the arena. The arena lies to the south-west of this point, so face that way with the steel player in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the sculpture and the arena fit in one frame. If the building won't fit, switch to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or higher (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the entrance towers or the big LED screen.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the sculpture on one third of the frame and let the arena fill the rest.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the red and gray building and the shiny sculpture are easy to read. A day without an event means fewer people walking through your picture.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie in Championship Plaza, beside the tall steel hockey player, which a Newark arena guide lists as a photo-worthy spot. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and turn so the player and as much of the arena as you can fit are over your shoulder. For a second try, stand beside the Martin Brodeur statue at the Lafayette Street entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the Prudential Center, so keep yours in your bag. Check the arena's access rules on the official site before you go, and expect a bit of a crowd on event days.
card.challenge: Can you get the hockey player and the whole arena in one shot without the building leaning? Keep the phone level and take a few steps back along Mulberry or Lafayette Street if you need to.
card.good_to_know: Prudential Center opened in 2007 and is home to the New Jersey Devils, the New York Sirens and Seton Hall's men's basketball team. Fans call it "The Rock" after the Rock of Gibraltar logo of Prudential Financial. The red and gray outside nods to Newark's bricklaying and railroad past, and the front LED screen is about 4,800 square feet.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Championship Plaza on Mulberry Street, between Edison Place and Market Street, right beside the arena. The arena lies to the south-west of this point, so face that way with the steel player in front of you.

card.hook: Most people charge through this building with one eye on the departures board. You're going to look up instead. It's one of the better-looking buildings in central Newark, and it's hiding in plain sight.
card.stand_here: Start near Raymond Boulevard, at the phone icon on the map, about 140 m north-west of the subject. Face south-east and the station is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x to fit the whole long stone frontage in one shot. Inside the waiting room, or if you're close to the building, switch to zoom 0.5x. Use zoom 2x or 5x for medallions, lamps and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the edges of the building up with them so the stonework doesn't lean. Then tap the brightest part of the facade and drag the slider a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on stonework. Mid-morning outside the commuter rush may be calmer inside. On a grey day the front can look flat, so go for the carved detail and the lamps instead.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and zoom 0.5x, hold your arm out a bit and tilt the phone up. That squeezes the stone frontage in behind your shoulder. Inside, the same trick works with the ceiling and chandeliers above you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working station, so keep to public areas and stay out of commuters' way. Check the official site for any photography rules. Avoid the Market Street exit late at night and use the Raymond Plaza exit instead.
card.challenge: Hunt down the medallions in the main waiting room and see if you can photograph a wagon, a steamship, a car and an aeroplane.
card.good_to_know: The station was designed by McKim, Mead & White, the architects behind the original Penn Station in New York, and it mixes Art Deco and Neo-Classical features. It was dedicated on 23 March 1935, and the south-eastern half was finished in 1937 after the older station was demolished. A big restoration in 2007 cleaned up the facade and the historic interior materials, including the plaster ceilings, marble and limestone.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start near Raymond Boulevard, at the phone icon on the map, about 140 m north-west of the subject. Face south-east and the station is right in front of you.

selfie_research.safety: Avoid the Market Street exit late at night and use the Raymond Plaza exit instead (pennstations.com, 'Newark Penn Station Guide (2026)').
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot or a passer-by spot for Newark Penn Station, so I have left both empty rather than guess. The Yelp, Foursquare and Tripadvisor results show interior photos only (waiting room, ceiling, zodiac chandeliers). The Art Deco facade on Raymond Boulevard and the arched portals with granite eagles over Market Street and Raymond Boulevard are described by historic-structures.com (Building Description, Pennsylvania Train Station), philaprrths.com (Penn Station Newark), and the NRHP nomination form, but none of them calls these a selfie or photo spot. A Subway Nut photo caption names 'The Market Street plaza and entrance to the station' (subwaynut.com/njt/newark_penn), which might be a candidate, but I could not confirm it as a photo spot. No page I found gives selfie-stick or tripod rules. The station's location is at 1 Raymond Plaza West (Amtrak page), which matches the given coordinates.

card.hook: This museum looks like several buildings that grew up side by side: a red brick former YMCA to the south, an 1885 house to the north, and a 1920s main block in the middle. Your photo's job is to show them all getting along.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Washington Park side of the museum, well back from the entrance, then turn around and face the building. The phone icon on the map marks the museum itself, which is too close for a full view.
card.zoom: At zoom 0.5x you can fit the whole width in from across the park, so start there. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then use 2x or 5x for doorways, brickwork and sculpture (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's upright edges up with them so it doesn't lean, and leave a strip of park or sky in the frame to show how big it is.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, ideally mid-morning or later in the afternoon. The light is softer then, and the front isn't squinting into harsh midday glare.
card.selfie_here: Go to the bronze NOW statue by Shahzia Sikander on the Ballantine House side of the museum. Use the front camera, stand beside the statue with the museum behind you, and check on arrival that the framing works.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of the main entrance, near Sanford Biggers' 'Apollo (Diptych)' sculpture, and ask a passer-by to take your photo with the doors behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash and selfie sticks aren't allowed in the museum galleries. Non-commercial photos are fine except where signs say otherwise.
card.challenge: Find the 1784 stone schoolhouse in the garden behind the museum and get it in the foreground, with the museum wall behind it. Old and new in one shot!
card.good_to_know: The main building was designed by Jarvis Hunt and opened in the 1920s after a gift from Louis Bamberger. Michael Graves redesigned much of it in 1990. The whole complex is around 149 m across, and the front doors reopened in 2018 with a ramp, so the entrance deserves a photo of its own.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Washington Park side of the museum, well back from the entrance, then turn around and face the building. The phone icon on the map marks the museum itself, which is too close for a full view.

card.hook: Picture a county park in Newark that turns pink and white every April, with more than 5,000 cherry trees doing it all at once. Yes, really, and it's the biggest blossom collection in the United States.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Cherry Blossom Welcome Center, in the grove of trees right outside it. Face in among the branches, and remember the main part of the park lies about 1.6 km to the south of it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the grove and your friends under the trees. Go to 2x or more to pick out a single branch of blossom, and 0.5x when you want the whole canopy overhead.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the blossom, then slide the brightness down a little so the pale petals keep their detail against a bright sky.
card.best_time: Peak bloom is typically the second and third week of April. The Welcome Center gets very crowded on festival weekends, so go early on a weekday if you can.
card.selfie_here: Grab a selfie among the densest cherry trees beside the Cherry Blossom Welcome Center, at the park's eastern end, so the blossom fills the frame behind you. For something calmer, try the path beside the water, with the lake and trees behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the outdoor photo area outside the Welcome Center while you stand under the trees, so the cherry grove and playground both fit in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: If you stay late, be mindful of who is around you after about 5 PM. Festival-time arrangements may vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a branch hanging low enough to frame your friend's face, then take the shot without anyone noticing you're being artistic.
card.good_to_know: Branch Brook Park opened in 1895 as the nation's first county park, and at 360 acres it's the largest public park in Newark. The first cherry trees came from a 1927 gift by Caroline Bamberger Fuld. Today there are more than 5,000 trees in over eighteen varieties.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Cherry Blossom Welcome Center, in the grove of trees right outside it. Face in among the branches, and remember the main part of the park lies about 1.6 km to the south of it.

card.hook: Picture a giant French Gothic cathedral rising over a city park, with the lawn doing the job of a front garden. That's Newark's Sacred Heart, and it's about the size of Westminster Abbey, so yes, it's big.
card.stand_here: Stand at the edge of Branch Brook Park, on the park side of the cathedral, and face back toward the west façade and its twin towers. This is the classic view of the whole building rising above the park.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both towers and some of the park in one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the towers and the big round rose window.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they don't lean, then tap the pale stonework and nudge the picture a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, around golden hour, is the sweet spot from the park's edge. In spring the cherry blossom season adds pink for your foreground.
card.selfie_here: Try the small paved courtyard in front of the main façade (89 Ridge St) with the towers behind you, or the lawn or path in Branch Brook Park across from the front. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it), hold it a bit low and let the towers rise over your shoulder. It's worth checking both spots on your map, as they're general areas rather than exact marks.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the park approach and shoot up toward the west façade and twin towers, while you pose in front of the cathedral with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral is a working place of worship, so check the official site for visiting arrangements before you go in. The main door is reported to be locked, with visitors asked to use the side entrance. If you go inside, skip the flash and don't disturb Mass or prayer.
card.challenge: Get a shot with pink blossom (in spring) or green lawn in the bottom third, both towers dead centre, and a little sky left on top. Bonus points if the rose window is easy to spot.
card.good_to_know: It's the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Newark and the fifth-largest cathedral in North America. Construction began in 1899 and finished in 1954, and the design switched from English-Irish Gothic Revival to French Gothic Revival along the way. The 36-foot rose window over the main entrance is described as the largest in the Catholic Church in the Western Hemisphere.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the edge of Branch Brook Park, on the park side of the cathedral, and face back toward the west façade and its twin towers. This is the classic view of the whole building rising above the park.

selfie_spots.why: A blogger chose this courtyard as the spot to photograph the façade, which suggests it gives a clear, unobstructed view of the building for a selfie with the cathedral behind.

card.hook: Picture a stone palace from 15th-century Florence, dropped into downtown Newark. That's the library's front, and it's a proper head-turner.
card.stand_here: Stand at the northern corner of Harriet Tubman Square (formerly Washington Park) and face north-west. The library is about 120 m to the north-west, straight across the open park.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole front in. If trees or people crowd you, try 0.5x. Then go 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for the entrance and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with them so the vertical lines stay nice and straight.
card.best_time: Check the light on the day, because the sky and the shadows on the front change as time goes by. Take a quick look at both before you set up, and if the sky is bright, tap the facade and slide it a little darker so the stone keeps its detail.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt it up a touch so the library sits big over your shoulder. Hold still for a second before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone at the northern corner of Harriet Tubman Square facing north-west, then stand a few steps ahead of them with the library behind you so the whole front fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The library is open to visitors, but check the official site before you go for opening times and any rules on photography inside.
card.challenge: Get two shots: one wide frame of the whole front with a strip of green park in front, then one close-up of a stone detail near the entrance. Bonus points if the vertical lines stay straight.
card.good_to_know: The Newark Public Library is at 5 Washington Street and opened in 1901. Rankin and Kellogg designed it, taking their inspiration from the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence. The Newark Museum was founded inside it in 1909.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the northern corner of Harriet Tubman Square (formerly Washington Park) and face north-west. The library is about 120 m to the north-west, straight across the open park.

ask_someone_spot.name: Northern corner of Washington Park
ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand at the northern corner of Washington Park, facing northwest toward the library, so the visitor stands between you and the building with the whole facade in frame. The source describes this as a spot for photographing the library, though it does not mention visitor photos.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the library directly behind the visitor, so I left selfie_spots empty rather than guess. The ask-someone spot rests on a 2009 Wikimedia photo taken from the northern corner of Washington Park, looking northwest at the Main Library (5 Washington St). It is a photographer's vantage point, not a stated photo-spot recommendation, so check it on the ground. Washington Park is across Washington Street from the library, per AAA and Yelp. The Yelp listing for 50 Hayes St is a different branch (Springfield) and was not used. No page I found states rules on selfie sticks or tripods, and no page gave a safety point for this spot. The search budget ran out before I could try another query.

card.hook: There's a real gold dome sitting in the middle of downtown Newark, and it catches the sky like it knows you're looking. Everything else on the street is glass and concrete, so it's hard to miss.
card.stand_here: Stand on Broad Street, on the sidewalk across from the front facade, and stay back from the building. City Hall is to the south-east of you, so face south-east and you'll see the whole building with its golden dome and columns, framed by trees and modern towers.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which should fit the whole building and dome. If you can't step back far enough, switch to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a close-up of the gold.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dome, then drag the brighter/darker slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail against a bright sky.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the dome shows up best. The gold really stands out against the sky and the towers behind it.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the foot of the main exterior stairwell on the front of the building, which has been used as a backdrop for group photos. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold your phone a bit higher, so you and as much of the building as possible fit in. For a different shot, pose next to the bronze George Floyd statue on the grounds outside the entrance.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to frame the facade from across the street on Franklin Street while you stand in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the public street, but access inside may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the dome in the top third of your frame with the columns standing straight on the gridlines, and see if you can keep the tilt out.
card.good_to_know: Newark City Hall is a five-storey Beaux Arts building, built in 1902. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on 17 February 1978. In 1986 the developer Harry Grant paid for the dome to be covered in 24 carat gold.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Broad Street, on the sidewalk across from the front facade, and stay back from the building. City Hall is to the south-east of you, so face south-east and you'll see the whole building with its golden dome and columns, framed by trees and modern towers.

selfie_research.notes: Thin sourcing: no page I found gives a camera position with the building directly behind the visitor, so the selfie spots are inferred from pages that show people posing or the statue as a photo subject; check on the ground. The stairwell page describes a photo shoot and does not say which way the camera faced. The Franklin Street spot is a Yelp photo caption ('the facade from Franklin St.'), not a written tip, so the exact standing point is unconfirmed. One guide says exterior photography is generally allowed for personal use but may be restricted inside government offices or during events; this is not a selfie stick or tripod rule, so it is not listed under rules. Military Park's Wars of America monument was found in searches but no page links it to a view of City Hall, so it is omitted.

card.hook: Newark's Broad Street is loud and busy, and then there's this calm stone church that's been standing since 1787, with a hotel right next door. Old and new in one frame, and you barely have to try.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Broad Street sidewalk outside 820 Broad Street, looking east toward the church. Face it straight on so the whole front fills your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the head-on view. If the tower and roofline won't fit, step back a bit instead of tilting your phone up, because tilting makes the walls lean. Use 0.5x only if traffic or the pavement stops you stepping back. Save 2x for the doorway and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the church's straight up-and-down edges against them, with a little sky above the roof.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime when the weather's clear, so you can see the church properly.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, keep your arm out, and turn so the church sits over your shoulder. Try 0.5x to squeeze more of the building in behind you, and keep your phone upright so the tower fits.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to shoot from the Broad Street sidewalk facing east, so the church fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Broad Street is busy, so stay on the sidewalk and take care when crossing. You can photograph the outside from the public sidewalk, but check the official site before visiting the grounds, the burial ground or the inside.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the Hotel Indigo building peeking in at the edge, and one with it cropped out. Which one feels more like Newark?
card.good_to_know: The church is now also known as First Church Newark, and it's part of the Four Corners Historic District. The building dates from 1787, and the grounds include an old burial ground where several people who served New Jersey in Congress are buried, including William Burnet and Silas Condit. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Broad Street sidewalk outside 820 Broad Street, looking east toward the church. Face it straight on so the whole front fills your screen.

ask_someone_spot.name: Broad Street sidewalk, looking east at the church (820 Broad Street)
ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand on the Broad Street sidewalk facing east so the church fills the frame. The source describes a photo taken this way, from Broad Street, of the church on a sunny midday. The church sits next to the Hotel Indigo, so keep that building out of the frame if you want the church alone.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot for this church, so selfie_spots is empty rather than filled from memory. The ask-someone spot is a photographer's vantage point from a 2009 Wikimedia upload, not a tourist photo guide, so treat it as a rough suggestion and check it on the ground. Sources give the address as 820 Broad Street; the Wikimedia photo coordinates sit close to the church's given position. No page I found mentions selfie sticks, tripods, or safety. The sources also contain no real-time information on access or photography restrictions at the church.

card.hook: A bronze charge of horses and soldiers is frozen in the middle of downtown Newark, and the path at its feet is shaped like a giant sword. It's about eighty yards long, so your photo practically composes itself.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on the sword-shaped walkway or the grass around the bronze, in the south-western part of Military Park. Face the raised granite base. The middle of the park lies to the north-east of the statue.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the bronze and its granite base. Switch to 0.5x to catch the whole sword-shaped walkway, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for close-ups of the horses and figures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the pedestal on a vertical line, then tap the bronze and slide a little darker so the metal keeps its detail against the bright sky.
card.best_time: No particular time is recommended for this spot. Seasonal outdoor dining, events and a carousel can wander into your frame, so wait a moment for a clear view if you want just the sculpture.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the Wars of America sculpture, standing on the sword-shaped walkway with the bronze behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone offers it) and hold it a bit low so the sculpture fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a public city park, but events and seasonal features can change what's open, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Crouch low and try to get the bronze rising against the sky with the downtown towers peeking out behind it.
card.good_to_know: Military Park is a six-acre green space, laid out by Robert Treat as a training ground for soldiers and later used as an army campground. The Wars of America bronze was made by Gutzon Borglum, the sculptor of Mount Rushmore. The park was renovated and reopened in June 2014.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, on the sword-shaped walkway or the grass around the bronze, in the south-western part of Military Park. Face the raised granite base. The middle of the park lies to the north-east of the statue.

selfie_spots.name: Wars of America sculpture, Military Park (on the sword-shaped walkway)
selfie_spots.detail: on the sword-shaped walkway set into the ground in the southwestern part of the park, with the bronze statue behind you
selfie_spots.why: Guides single out this sculpture as the park's standout photo subject, and a scavenger-hunt guide tells players to snap a selfie with the sword-wielding warrior.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot is supported by the pages I found; no page names a second spot. The sword-shaped walkway detail comes from a Locations Hub entry (the monument is in the southwest part of the park and the sword is built into the ground) and an Arts Adventurer blog (the sword-shaped pavement sits lower than the surrounding grass). No page names a specific standing point for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole sculpture, so ask_someone_spot is null; the Wikimedia photo pages give only coordinates and compass headings, which are not named places. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules, and no page mentions a safety point for this site. Some sources are old (one blog is about 1,200 days old), and the Yelp hours shown are inconsistent across listings, so check current hours before visiting.

card.hook: Picture a row of grand houses facing a park, then picture all but one of them gone. The salmon-coloured brick of the John Ballantine House is what's left, and it glows against the park's greenery.
card.stand_here: Cross Washington Street towards Washington Park, then turn back to face the John Ballantine House. You'll have room to fit the whole front in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the full front from across the street. Only drop to 0.5x if you're close and can't fit it all in. Then try 2x for the portico and the brick and stone details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line up the middle gabled bay with the centre line, and tap the brick wall, then slide darker if the sky is bright so the salmon colour stays rich.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the front of the house is likely to be lit. A soft, bright overcast day also makes the brick look great.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the brick front over your shoulder so it fills the background. Hold the phone upright and keep it level so the walls don't lean.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch for passing cars and parked vehicles when you line up the wide view. The house is a museum open for tours, so check the official site before you go. You can photograph the outside from the street and park.
card.challenge: Count the five uneven bays across the front, then get one shot with the arches of the portico framing something green from the park.
card.good_to_know: The house was built in 1884 for John Holme Ballantine and his wife Jeannette Boyd. He was the son of the founder of the Ballantine beer brewery. It was once one of several grand houses facing the park and is now the only one left. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1985 and reopened in November 2023 after a restoration.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Cross Washington Street towards Washington Park, then turn back to face the John Ballantine House. You'll have room to fit the whole front in.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the John Ballantine House behind the visitor, or a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole house in frame, so both fields are empty. The pages only describe the building: it stands on the west side of Washington Street, facing Washington Park near its southern edge (https://dspace.njstatelib.org/items/bcae58b1-ed59-4c19-9a5d-903b3a997b04). A page on the Ballantine House's exterior calls it a charming backdrop, and says the surrounding museum grounds can also provide nice shots, but it names no specific place (https://www.airial.travel/attractions/united-states/newark/ballantine-house-EajjPSqL). Washington Park is named, but no page calls it a photo spot, so I did not use it. No page mentions selfie sticks, tripods, or safety. One page says non-flash photography is generally permitted inside for personal use and flash is generally not allowed, which is an interior rule rather than a selfie-stick rule, so I left it out of 'rules' (same Airial source). Address conflict: the Newark Museum and Kiddle list 49 Washington Street, while the Library of Congress HABS record lists 43 Washington Street. The Wikimedia Commons coordinates (40.833, -74.171) do not match the position you gave (40.74318, -74.17123), so check the map pin before relying on it. Locals could verify a good spot in person or on a current photo map.

card.hook: Picture a huge vertical PARAMOUNT sign soaring over a Newark street, with a big NEWARK marquee underneath. It's a bold, moody old movie palace, and it's the kind of place that makes you stop mid-stride.
card.stand_here: Stand on Market Street in front of the theatre at 195 Market Street, facing the facade, a short way east of the Market and Broad Street crossing. If you happen to be inside the Prudential Center, the glass-walled concourse gives you a higher view down onto the roofline and signage.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole facade with the street in front of it. If the pavement is narrow and the sign won't fit, try zoom 0.5x, then 2x to pick out the lettering and marquee detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the tall sign up with a vertical line so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the sign and marquee read clearly and you can see what's going on around you. Pick a quieter moment if you want fewer cars and people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x so more of the building squeezes in, and tilt the phone up a touch so the sign towers over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The theatre is closed and derelict, so don't try to go inside or climb on any fencing. If you step back across the road to fit the sign in, watch for passing traffic.
card.challenge: Get the sign and the marquee in one frame with a strip of street at the bottom, and keep the sign dead straight. Bonus points if no car photobombs you.
card.good_to_know: The theatre opened in 1886, closed in 1986, and took the Paramount name around 1930. Billie Holiday performed here, and Jerry Lewis worked as an usher when he was young. Its facade was even dressed up as the 'New Art' cinema in the 2019 film Joker, and redevelopment plans say the facade and marquee are to be kept and restored, so it may look different when you visit.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Market Street in front of the theatre at 195 Market Street, facing the facade, a short way east of the Market and Broad Street crossing. If you happen to be inside the Prudential Center, the glass-walled concourse gives you a higher view down onto the roofline and signage.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the Newark Paramount Theatre behind the visitor, or a passer-by spot for photographing a visitor with the whole building. The pages I found are mostly history, photo archives, art prints, and a redevelopment story. Useful background: <cite index="6-10">the former Paramount Theatre still boasts the vertical 'Paramount' sign, as well as the 'Newark' marquee</cite>, and it sits at <cite index="17-2">195 Market Street, a half block from the intersection of Broad and Market Streets</cite>. A Cinema Treasures comment says <cite index="4-2">you can get a good clear elevated view of the Paramount from inside the glass walled concourse</cite>, but it does not name the building, so I did not use it. Redevelopment is also planned: <cite index="16-14">the historic façade with its notable marquee will be stabilized and fully restored</cite>, so the marquee view may change. No selfie-stick or tripod rules were found. Sources checked: cinematreasures.org/theaters/4603, afterthefinalcurtain.net/2011/09/28/the-newark-paramount-theatre/, thestrawfoot.com/2018/05/20/a-walk-past-the-newark-paramount/, jerseydigs.com (Paramount redevelopment story). A local visitor guide or Newark tourism page would be the next place to look.

card.hook: Most statues make you look way up. This Lincoln sits down, tosses his stovepipe hat beside him and leaves you room on the bench.
card.stand_here: Head for Essex County Courthouse Plaza. The statue is about 1 minute on foot to the south-east, beside the courthouse steps. Face west toward Lincoln so the courthouse fills the space behind him.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get Lincoln and the courthouse together. Try zoom 2x for a closer shot of his face (higher zooms depend on your phone), or zoom 0.5x if you stand close and want the whole bench and steps.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bronze, then nudge the brightness slider darker if the sky behind is washing him out, because bronze looks best a little darker.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives you soft light that suits bronze better than harsh midday sun. Early in the day there are also likely to be fewer people on the courthouse steps.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the free end of Lincoln's bench, near the Springfield Avenue and Market Street corner, and use the front camera. Lincoln ends up beside you rather than behind you, so tilt the phone to squeeze in his face and hat.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the courthouse plaza east of the statue, facing west, while you sit by Lincoln so the courthouse is in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go in case there are access or security restrictions around the courthouse. Street furniture and fencing can change, so take a quick look at the layout when you arrive.
card.challenge: Get Lincoln's hat, the bench and your grin all in one frame, like he just stepped away for a coffee.
card.good_to_know: Gutzon Borglum made this larger-than-life bronze, unveiled in 1911. He took the idea from accounts of Lincoln sitting alone on a bench to think during the Civil War. Theodore Roosevelt is said to have remarked at the unveiling that it didn't look like a monument at all.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Essex County Courthouse Plaza. The statue is about 1 minute on foot to the south-east, beside the courthouse steps. Face west toward Lincoln so the courthouse fills the space behind him.

selfie_research.notes: No source ranks selfie angles, so 'best' here means the most-documented positions. The 'ask someone' spot is inferred: the 1994 NRHP photo list gives a view looking west with the courthouse in the background, but the photographer's exact placement east of the statue is my reading, not stated. The stairs spot's visitor position is also inferred from a photo taken from the stairs. The Reconstruction Era page is about 3 years old, and the NRHP form dates from 1994. card.hook: Picture a 22-foot bronze lamp post standing over two marble figures, a Native American and a Puritan. It's the same sculptor who made Mount Rushmore, and it's just sitting there in a Newark park.
card.stand_here: Stand in Harriet Tubman Square (it used to be called Washington Park), at the north end where the monument now stands. Face north-east, so the statue sits in the park with downtown Newark rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the statue with the city behind it. Switch to 0.5x only if you're close and need the whole 22-foot standard, then use 2x to fill the frame with the marble figures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the lamp standard on one vertical line so it stands up straight.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the dark bronze and pale marble than harsh midday sun. Early on a weekday is likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the tip of Harriet Tubman Square, on the library side of the monument, so the statue is behind you and the Newark Public Library is in front. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone up a little so the bronze standard fits over your shoulder. Nobody has confirmed this exact spot, so check it when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Washington Street, opposite the Newark Public Library at 5 Washington Street, while you stand by the monument, so the whole thing fits in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is an open public space, but check the signs on the ground in case anything has changed.
card.challenge: Find Newark's city seal on the lamp standard and get it in one shot along with a figure below.
card.good_to_know: Gutzon Borglum made this monument in 1916 for Newark's 250th anniversary, which covered 1666 to 1916. It was moved to its present spot in 1977 and has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1994. The marble figures show some wear and vandalism, so a shot of the full lamp standard against the streets makes a good second picture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Harriet Tubman Square (it used to be called Washington Park), at the north end where the monument now stands. Face north-east, so the statue sits in the park with downtown Newark rising behind it.

selfie_spots.name: Harriet Tubman Square, north tip of the park facing the Newark Public Library
selfie_spots.detail: at the tip of the square, on the library side of the monument, so the statue is behind you and the library is in front of you
selfie_spots.why: Pages say the monument now faces the Newark Public Library, so standing between the statue and the library should put the sculpture behind a visitor, though no page names a selfie position.
